newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judge probes three ex-government ministers.
newsitem.headline: French judge probes three ex-government ministers.

text.p: A French judge has placed three centrist former government ministers under investigation in a probe into illegal party funding, justice sources said on Wednesday.

They said Jacques Barrot, labour minister in the outgoing government, former justice minister Pierre Mehaignerie and former transport minister Bernard Bosson were put under investigation by Paris judge Jean-Pierre Zanoto on Monday.

Barrot, Mehaignerie, and Bosson were all re-elected on Sunday after a campaign in which sleaze was a major issue, with the left accusing Gaullist President Jacques Chirac of calling the election almost 10 months early to pre-empt mounting scandals affecting his Rally For the Republic (RPR) party.

The three former members of the Force Democrate party, as well as a former treasurer of the group which is part of the wider Union for French Democracy (UDF) coalition party, were suspected of illicit party financing, the sources said.
The four are suspected of creating a slush fund in Switzerland to channel illicit funds into the party.

The sources said Jean Arthuis, finance minister in the outgoing government, was initially mentioned in the case but the judge was considering clearing him because his role in the party had been too minor.
"I was not one of the leaders, I was not treasurer of the party. This does not concern me," Arthuis said in April.
The centre-right, made up of the RPR and the UDF, was defeated in Sunday's parliamentary election which brought a leftist bloc led by the Socialists to power.
On Tuesday, a prosecutor opened an investigation into suspected graft over public works contracts by the Paris regional council, led by a Chirac ally.

The Paris public prosecutor's office launched the investigation into the Ile de France council, led by Michel Giraud, for "favouritism, fraud, forgery, receiving the proceeds of fraud and anti-competitive practices in public tenders".
Giraud is a senior member of Chirac's RPR. Chirac was mayor of Paris until his election as president in 1995.

A regional auditors' report sent to Giraud on April 8 condemned "practices aimed at restraining competition", especially in awards of building high schools in the Ile de France region which includes Paris and surroundings.
But the Paris prosecutor, Gabriel Bestard, had put off an immediate decision on whether to open a probe.
The Greens group in the regional council complained last year that Giraud's council had awarded a string of contracts to a single consultancy firm, Patrimoine Ingenierie, from 1989-94.
It said 171 of 212 such consultancy contracts went to the company, worth a total of 319.5 million francs ($54 million).
In a string of scandals involving awards of public contracts and politics in France, rake-offs are suspected of going back into party coffers. All major parties have been tainted by corruption.
